layers.name: Kernel Layer
layers.description: Cross-cutting leaf modules in packages/core/src/kernel/ (fqn-codec, prisma-client, db-connection, enum-validation, identity-guard-installer, lexical-search, alias-resolver, registry, schema-version, search-diagnostics, types, and the newly added sanitize/credential-scrub) that any tier may import while importing no tier itself -- confirmed by the import graph, which shows zero outgoing edges to any other tier (only 5 internal kernel-to-kernel edges) and 98 incoming edges from Services (60), Data (27), and Tools (11) combined.

layers.name: Tool Handlers Layer
layers.description: Thin MCP tool-handler modules in packages/core/src/tools/ (schema plus delegation, no business logic) -- the outermost entry surface of the product's business-logic package, calling down into the Service Layer (41 import edges) and directly into Kernel (11) and Data (1); both transports invoke this layer rather than Services directly.

layers.name: Service Layer
layers.description: The dominant domain-logic and orchestration layer in packages/core/src/services/ -- search, synapse, structural parsing, memory, memory-graph, embeddings, jobs, executor, scheduler, symbol graph, project-identity, hooks, etl, context, checkpoint, cache, web, workspace, events, handoff, compression, indexing, bootstrap, monitoring, metrics, pricing, vector, and health -- plus the package-root barrel (src/index.ts) re-exporting the whole public surface; the largest and most internally cohesive layer (intra-group import density 0.394), also holding the five orchestrators that moved here when the Controllers Layer was retired.

layers.name: Data Layer
layers.description: PostgreSQL/pgvector persistence in packages/core/src/data/ (symbol, memory, memory-graph generation, audit, handoff, proposal, keyword/FTS, managed-runs, vector store, plus a deadlock-retry wrapper), the data-model types in src/models/ (CacheEntry, CompressedContent), and the package-root Prisma CLI config (prisma.config.ts) -- a leaf tier confirmed by the import graph, which shows Data importing only Kernel (27 edges) and never Services.

layers.name: Test Layer
layers.description: All 416 test files across every package -- packages/core's centralized src/__tests__/ tree (325 files, including the e2e/ suite with its 29 single-file polyglot grammar fixtures for the tree-sitter structural parser, plus integration/, fixtures/, helpers/, and test-seam/ subdirectories, now also holding the new credential-scrub.test.ts and helpers/rss-delta.ts), packages/shared's split convention (a top-level __tests__/ plus a nested config/__tests__/), and every co-located *.test.ts sibling in apps/tools-api/src/routes, middleware, and src root, apps/mcp-client/src root, and each app's own __tests__/ directory -- kept as one cross-cutting layer since test files are scattered by both centralized and co-located convention and cannot be cheaply attributed back to a single subject layer.

layers.name: Shared Utility Layer
layers.description: packages/shared/src/ -- the runtime config loader (config/, reading ~/.config/massa-ai/config.json plus XDG/env/API-key handling), shared utils (logger, rate-limiter, tokenizer, sanitizer, metrics, benchmark), and shared TypeScript types (structural-transport, interfaces) -- the cross-cutting package consumed by core and every app transport.

layers.name: REST API Transport
layers.description: apps/tools-api/src/ -- the Elysia REST server on :3333 (route handlers in routes/, auth/error middleware, and startup/health bootstrap wiring), one of the two transports over the single tool contract, and the mount point for the Web UI dashboard at /ui.

layers.name: MCP Stdio Transport
layers.description: apps/mcp-client/src/ -- the MCP stdio server exposing 52 tools via tool-def JSON Schemas (tool-defs/) and the dual api-client/embedded-api-client clients behind ToolProxyApiClient, the second of the two transports over the same contract.

layers.name: Auxiliary App Surfaces
layers.description: Two smaller install/runtime surfaces beyond the two primary transports -- apps/web-ui's dashboard (static JS/CSS/HTML served at /ui) and apps/opencode-plugin's in-process OpenCode plugin handlers (observation-emitter, session-project-pin, config-cli).

tour.title: Core Architecture Barrel
tour.description: massa-ai is a monorepo with no single README node in this graph, so the tour starts at the file that plays that role instead: the root barrel of @massa-ai/core. It re-exports the package's entire public surface — tools, services, data repositories, and kernel types — as a single transport-independent business-logic entry point. This one file is the map for the whole tour: everything downstream is one of the four tiers it names, and both apps covered in Steps 2-3 import from it rather than reimplementing logic themselves.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript barrel files re-export an entire module tree through `export * from './submodule'` statements, giving consumers one import path (`@massa-ai/core`) instead of dozens of deep relative imports — at the cost of making it harder to see which specific file a symbol actually lives in.

tour.title: REST API Transport
tour.description: The Tools API is one of two transports wrapping the core barrel from Step 1 in a network-facing protocol: an Elysia HTTP server on port 3333 that bootstraps CORS, Swagger docs, roughly twenty route groups, a stale-job reaper, and a scheduler. Every route outside a small public allowlist requires an `x-api-key` header, enforced by the auth middleware shown here, which resolves or provisions the key once at startup and derives an actor identity used for audit-log attribution. This is the transport a browser, curl, or any non-MCP client uses to reach the same business logic Step 1 described.
tour.languageLesson: Allowlist-based auth middleware (deny-by-default, with a short list of explicitly public paths) is safer than blocklist-based auth: a newly added route is protected automatically, since you have to opt a route out of auth rather than remember to opt it in.

tour.title: MCP Stdio Transport
tour.description: The second transport speaks the Model Context Protocol over stdio instead of HTTP — the integration surface for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode. Its entry point proxies ListTools/CallTool requests to the same Tools API from Step 2, choosing between an HTTP client and an in-process embedded client depending on configuration. tool-definitions.ts is the facade that concatenates per-domain tool-def modules (search, memory, synapse, project, hooks-exec) into the single ordered array of 52 tool schemas the MCP protocol advertises to a connecting agent.
tour.languageLesson: MCP tools are described declaratively as JSON Schema, not as live function references — a ListTools call returns pure data and CallTool dispatches by name, which is what lets one schema definition serve two different underlying transports (HTTP vs. embedded in-process) without the calling agent knowing the difference.

tour.title: Shared Utility Package
tour.description: Both transports from Steps 2-3, and the core package from Step 1, depend on one more package before any business logic runs: @massa-ai/shared. Its root barrel re-exports an environment-loader side effect, shared types and interfaces, a utils barrel, and the full configuration module — covering defaults, XDG paths, and API-key resolution. Centralizing configuration in one package rather than duplicating it across core and each app is what lets every transport agree on the same runtime settings.
tour.languageLesson: Importing a module purely for its side effects (`import './env-loader'` with no bound names) is a deliberate ESM pattern for run-once setup code — the barrel re-exports it first in file order so the side effect fires before anything that reads the resulting environment.

tour.title: Kernel: The Leaf Tier
tour.description: Before following the tools -> services -> data flow that Step 1's barrel named, meet the one tier that sits outside it: kernel/. Every other tier may import kernel, and kernel imports nothing back — prisma-client.ts, the shared Prisma singleton wrapping PostgreSQL, is in fact the single most depended-upon file in the entire codebase, with 50 other files importing it directly. kernel/types.ts sits beside it, defining the canonical structural taxonomy (symbol kinds, edge kinds, capability tiers) and the versioned, discriminated-union parse-outcome types that every structural and ETL consumer downstream shares. Understanding these two files first makes the data model in every later step legible.
tour.languageLesson: Discriminated unions — a shared 'kind' literal field that TypeScript narrows on — let a single ParseOutcome type safely represent several different result shapes (success, partial, failure) while the compiler forces every consumer to handle each case explicitly.

tour.title: Tools: Thin MCP Handlers
tour.description: tools/ is the outermost tier inside core — the layer both transports from Steps 2-3 actually call into, sitting directly below the MCP/HTTP boundary. Its barrel aggregates every tool implementation (indexing and search, memory CRUD, checkpoints, symbol-graph navigation, file reading, the polyglot code executor, an SSRF-guarded web fetch tool) behind one import surface, deliberately holding schema and delegation rather than business logic. serialize.ts is the shared response formatter every one of those handlers uses — dotted-path field projection plus TOON/JSON/tree encoding — which is why tool responses look consistent no matter which handler produced them.

tour.title: Services and the Indexing Pipeline
tour.description: services/ is where Step 6's tool handlers delegate their actual logic, and its barrel is the single largest hub in the graph — 76 outgoing imports, more than any other file — re-exporting search, memory, context, executor, symbol/graph, structural, jobs, scheduler, and synapse. Before touring those subsystems individually, meet the pipeline that feeds all of them: etl/pipeline.ts runs discover -> parse -> resolve -> load as a singleton orchestrator, coordinating a graph-generation lease and an optional managed-run lease with independent heartbeats, and invalidating the search cache and vector store once it completes. This is literally how 'indexing a codebase' happens — everything from Step 8 onward either feeds this pipeline or queries what it produced.
tour.languageLesson: Lease-based coordination — a time-bounded claim renewed by a heartbeat — lets exactly one worker own a long-running job across process restarts: if the heartbeat stops, the lease expires and another worker can safely take over instead of the job hanging forever.

tour.title: Polyglot Structural Parsing
tour.description: The 'parse' stage of Step 7's pipeline is powered by this subsystem, which wraps native tree-sitter to extract symbols from source files across many languages. language-manifest.ts maps every supported file extension to its grammar artifact, dialect, and capability tier (full structural extraction vs. lighter flow-only parsing), and resolves ambiguous cases like C/C++ headers. grammar-loaders.ts then loads the native grammar packages themselves, serializing a process-wide Bun-version compatibility mask so concurrent loads during a large index run can't race on that shared mutation — together they're why massa-ai's symbol graph in Step 10 isn't limited to TypeScript.
tour.languageLesson: Native Node/Bun addons — compiled tree-sitter grammars here — are process-global state, so two async loads racing to initialize the same native module can corrupt each other; that's why grammar-loaders.ts explicitly serializes its compatibility check instead of trusting normal async concurrency.

tour.title: Hybrid Search and Embeddings
tour.description: Once Step 7's pipeline and Step 8's parser have populated the index, this is how a query actually retrieves results. contextual-search-rlm.ts is the main search facade — 24 files depend on it and it in turn touches 20 others — but rather than implementing retrieval itself, it assembles per-call dependency records and delegates to single-purpose capability modules; hybrid-search.ts is the one that actually runs the vector+keyword pipeline with Reciprocal Rank Fusion, query correction, and proximity re-ranking. Underneath the vector half sits provider.ts, which unifies OpenAI, Google, Cohere, Ollama, and other backends behind one EmbeddingProvider interface, matching the project's local-first design where Ollama is the free, offline default.
tour.languageLesson: Reciprocal Rank Fusion merges two independently-ranked result lists (vector similarity and keyword match) using only each item's rank position, not its raw score — sidestepping the problem that a cosine-similarity score and a BM25 score live on incomparable scales.

tour.title: Symbol Graph Centrality
tour.description: This is the third pillar the project promises: a symbol graph ranked by dependency centrality, not just a flat index. The symbol/ barrel exposes definition lookup, reference and dependency graphs, PageRank centrality, Louvain community detection, architecture-map generation, and change-impact analysis; symbol-graph.service.ts is the high-level API (go-to-definition, references, dependency graph) sitting on top of it. It reaches persistence through data/symbol/symbol-repository-factory.ts, a factory guarding on a configured DATABASE_URL — a concrete example of the services -> data boundary Step 1's barrel promised, crossed cleanly through one factory function rather than a direct query.
tour.languageLesson: PageRank (originally for ranking web pages by inbound-link importance) and Louvain community detection (finding densely-connected clusters in a graph) are general-purpose graph algorithms repurposed here to rank source files by centrality in the dependency graph and cluster related files automatically.

tour.title: Memory and Synapse
tour.description: Where Step 10's symbol graph indexes code structure, this subsystem indexes the assistant's own decisions and observations — the project's fourth pillar, persistent cross-session memory. services/memory/index.ts exposes MemoryService for storing and scoring memories plus duplicate/redundancy filtering and semantic clustering; services/memory-graph/index.ts extends that with a Postgres-backed relation graph connecting memories to each other, so memories form a queryable network rather than a flat list. services/synapse/index.ts sits above both as the cognitive-modulation layer, lazily constructing a SynapseManager singleton from runtime config to handle query classification and session-level state — the mechanism that lets an assistant using massa-ai forget nothing between sessions, as the project describes it.

tour.title: Passive-Capture Hooks and Credential Scrubbing
tour.description: This step follows one feature through all four of core's tiers at once — a fitting capstone for the tools -> services -> data -> kernel architecture Step 1 named. hook-service.ts is the ingestion point for lifecycle events from Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and OpenCode's passive-capture hooks (the README's own phrase), validating each event, resolving which project it belongs to, and enqueueing persistence through a single-writer queue rather than blocking the caller. Before anything is written, every payload passes through credential-scrub.ts, a new Kernel-tier module alongside Step 5's prisma-client.ts and types.ts, which regex-redacts PEM keys, JWTs, and AWS/GitHub/Slack/bearer tokens and hands back a branded 'proof of sanitization' value rather than a boolean flag. The scrubbed result is persisted through observation-repository-pg.ts against the ObservationStore contract observation-contract.ts defines (Data tier, the same kind of persistence Step 10 used for the symbol graph), then read back out through compact_snapshot.ts — a Tools-tier MCP handler (Step 6) that returns a bounded, reference-based table of contents instead of inlined data, deliberately distinct from the checkpoints Step 6 also names.
tour.languageLesson: TypeScript's structural typing treats any two `string` values as interchangeable, so nothing stops a raw, unscrubbed payload from being passed where sanitized text is expected. Branding a type — widening a primitive with a phantom marker, so a `SanitizedPayloadJson` is a `string` but not just any `string` — turns that mistake into a compile error, because the only legal way to produce a value of the branded type is to call the function that performs the sanitization.

tour.title: Background Jobs and Auto-Improve
tour.description: Closing the tour is the job subsystem that runs everything from Step 7's ETL pipeline in the background. index-job-tracker.ts is an in-memory singleton tracking async indexing jobs through their lifecycle (create, update, heartbeat, complete), persisting each via a pluggable JobStore and publishing state changes on the event bus, with stale-job reaping if a heartbeat goes silent. auto-improve-job.ts builds on that same job infrastructure for a different purpose — a loop that detects patterns and proposes improvements a human then approves or rejects, persisted through data/proposal/proposal-repository.ts, the data-layer counterpart Step 10 showed for the symbol graph — a fitting final stop where the indexing, search, and memory machinery toured so far feeds a human reviewing what the system learned.
tour.languageLesson: A publish/subscribe event bus decouples a job's lifecycle from whatever needs to react to it — index-job-tracker.ts publishes state changes without knowing who's listening, so new consumers (a UI progress bar, a log, a metrics counter) can subscribe later without the tracker itself changing.
